utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Mathias Neuner and Daryl Mundis, assisted today by Mr. Andres Vatter, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber would like to greet everybody on the 25th of January, 2005. We would like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution, of the Defence, as well as everybody else in the courtroom and in the public gallery. Before we bring the next witness into the courtroom, we need to deal with the issue of exhibits. I'm going to give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence would like to tender the following documents into evidence: They are all on our list. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. These documents have been shown to the witness. I'm turning to the Prosecution. Do you have anything to say, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have three big categories of documents. The first one bears the mark T -- this is 1671 [as interpreted], and the English translation, this is part of the large group of three documents. The next one is DH1920. I apologise. There has been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. There has been an error with regard to the first document. The transcript reads that the document is 1671. It is actually 1871.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second document will be DH1920, and its translation into English will be DH1920/E. DH1603 will be admitted, with its English translation, 1603/E. We will also admit the 15 documents that are as follows: DH1994. The date is 16 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the date.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The -- 1994/E. Then 1995. This is a series of 11 reports of which the first bears the date 1st November 1993. Its English translation will be 1995/E. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. So we have given numbers to all of these exhibits, and the last one has been marked for identification. That's number 1936. And as far as the list under number 5 is concerned, this is a series of documents; however, those documents are only in B/C/S. I suppose you will be tendering them through some other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the first list of documents in keeping with your decision has already been marked for identification. Since they do not have a translation, we did not ask for another marked for identification. When we receive their translation, we will ask for their admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Usher, can you please bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. Please tell me whether you can hear the interpretation of what I am saying. If so, say that you understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have been called as a witness for the Defence. Before you make the solemn declaration, I will ask you to tell us your first and last name and your place and date of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Esed Sipic. I was born on the 17th of May, 1962 in the village of Siprag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation? Are you employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a professional soldier in the army of the federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, did you have an occupation and were you a professional soldier at that time? If so, what unit were you in and what rank did you hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, in the Territorial Defence initially. We did not have ranks in the army at that time. I was a former professional soldier in the JNA, and I was carrying out certain duties in the Territorial Defence in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1993, what unit were you in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, I was in two units: First, in 1993, up to mid-August, I was commander of the 306th Brigade. After mid-August, I was in the Bosnian Krajina OG.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Colonel, please tell us, have you ever testified before an international or national court about the events in your country in 1992 and 1993, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will now ask you to read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, before I give the floor to the Defence counsel, whom you will have met while preparing for this session, I must give you some information as to the manner in which these proceedings will take place. First of all, you are expected to testify today, and if your testimony is not completed, you will continue tomorrow afternoon. Initially you will answer the questions put to you by the counsel for the Defence, sitting on your left-hand side, and this is what we call the examination-in-chief. Direct questions will be put to you. After that, the representatives of the Prosecution, sitting on your right-hand side, will put questions to you, and this will be the cross-examination. If necessary, the Prosecutor can also put leading questions to you. Finally, both these stages will last for an equal length of time, and then you may be asked questions in redirect by the Defence counsel in connection with issues arising during the cross-examination. When all this is over, the three Judges sitting on the Bench, if they feel it necessary, may also put questions to you. As a rule, the Judges ask questions either because they wish to clarify certain points or because they consider that your replies were not exhaustive enough. After we put our questions to you, the two parties will again have the floor and they will be able to ask you questions on matters arising from the questions of the Judges. As you are a Defence witness, the witness [sic] will be the last to put any further questions they deem necessary. That is how today's session will proceed. I wish to draw your attention to a few other matters. You have now made the solemn declaration, and as you know, you and every other witness is duty-bound to tell the truth. False testimony is an offence, and this Court may take certain steps should anyone testify falsely. Secondly - and this is in our Rules of Procedure and Evidence - when replying to a question, you have the right not to answer the question if you feel that your response might one day in the future incriminate you in some way. You can, should this happen, tell the Judges you do not wish to answer the question. In this case, the Chamber may require you to answer the question, and in this case the Chamber will guarantee that your question will not later be used against you. It will not incriminate you. So you will be granted a certain kind of immunity. This is clearly stated in our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Apart from a very brief summary of your testimony, we know nothing about you. We have no documents about you. Your replies will be interpreted into English, and you have before you a monitor in which you can see everything that is being said in this courtroom, and your replies therefore will be the basis for the examination-in-chief, the cross-examination, and the Judges' questions. Your answers are very important. If you do not understand a question, please ask whoever put the question to you to reformulate it. Questions may at times be very complex, and you might find yourself in a situation that -- in which you're unable to answer. It's possible that during the examination one of the parties will put a document to you - most probably a military document - in order to learn what your comments on this document are. This is a general outline -- a broad outline of what your testimony will look like. Should you have any difficulties, please do not hesitate to tell us. We will have a break every hour and a half for technical reasons, and this will give you an opportunity to take a 25-minute break, a 25-minute rest, as will the interpreters, who are doing a very difficult and exhausting job and therefore they need a break. Today the sitting will last until 1900 hours and we will have two 25-minute breaks. Broadly speaking, this is what today's hearing will look like. I tell every witness this information. I will now give the floor to the Defence, who will give you some technical instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Sipic.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The President has just told you how important the work of the interpreters is. You and I speak the same language, and you can answer my question right away without making a pause. However, it's very important for my question to be interpreted for Their Honours and for my learned friends, and it is also very important for your reply to be interpreted. This is how we can best assist the Court to follow your testimony. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, please tell me, what education did you have before the war and what is your education today?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: In 1978, I enrolled in the secondary military school in Sarajevo, which lasted for four years, and I completed it in 1982. After this, I was assigned to a duty in the former JNA. During my work in the former JNA, in 1988 I enrolled in the military academy in Belgrade, where I graduated in 1991. After the war, I enrolled in the faculty of political sciences, and I graduated in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where did you live before the war and where did you work as a professional soldier before the war?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: As a professional soldier, before the war I lived in the Republic of Slovenia, which was part of Yugoslavia, in the town of Kopar, and I lived there until August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, why and with whom did you leave there in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: As everyone probably knows, in 1991, in August, the Yugoslav People's Army withdrew from the territory of the Republic of Slovenia and became dislocated. My unit was transferred to Travnik municipality. I arrived in Travnik with my unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, did there come a time when you left the JNA? When and why?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes. I left the former JNA in March 1991 because I could see that it was no longer the Yugoslav People's Army. It was no longer the army in which I had been educated and worked; that it was now a pro-Serb army representing the interests of only the Serbs in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After you left the army or that -- rather, the JNA, where did you go? And did you join any other armed force?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: As I was in Travnik, as soon as I left the former JNA I reported to the Municipal Territorial Defence Staff in Travnik in March 1992. I was received by the then-commander of the TO Municipal Staff, Mr. Zijan Caber.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, how long did you stay in the Municipal Staff? Were you transferred to another duty? And if so, how long did you perform this other duty?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: I remained in the Municipal Staff of the Travnik Territorial Defence until November 1992. After this, there were big changes. There was a big reorganisation of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And in November 1992, pursuant to an order by the commander of the Supreme Command, I became the commander of the 306th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, after you were appointed commander of the 306th Mountain Brigade, did you come across any problems or was this a simple Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and easy job?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: When the order was issued that the 306th Mountain Brigade was to be established, it was supposed to be a manoeuvring unit, an ex-territorial one. However, under the then-conditions it was impossible to establish such a brigade, a brigade such as the one envisaged. Rather, we had to establish it as a territorial unit in the Biljanska Dolina area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And who became part of the 306th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to an order of the General Command of the General Staff of Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the detachments existing in the Biljanska valley before, and these were Han Bila, Mehuric, Ljuta Greda, the 1st Siprage Battalion, and the Hum Detachment, they were all to become part of the 306th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, did all these units that were there in the Bila Valley enter into the composition of the 306th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: No. As I have already said, I did have some problems in establishing this brigade. These were not the only problems. There was also the problem of the Mehuric Detachment, which was later called Gluha Bukovica. We did not want to become part of the 306th Brigade. Rather, they demanded that they become part of the 314th Motorised Brigade. Later on there was an additional order from the Supreme Command that the Mehuric Detachment was to be part of the 314th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, the men of military age in the Bila River Valley, were they the men used to bring up the manpower levels of the 306th Mountain Brigade alone or other brigades as well?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: The men from the Bila River Valley joined not only the 306th but also the 314th Motorised Brigade, the 312th Motorised Brigade, the 17th Krajina Brigade, the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What about the replenishment of the brigade and its equipment? Was the brigade up to its strength?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: It is a well-known fact that this area is rather poor and people there were mostly engaged in cattle raising and agriculture. There were no people with either military experience or education save for a couple of exceptions, and those were people that made up the brigade. As for the materiel and technical equipment, we had very little because we didn't have any means to obtain any equipment, so I would say that the brigade was not up to its strength either when it came to men or -- and especially when it came to equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since I'm going to show the witness some documents, I would kindly ask the usher to distribute the binders that have been prepared for this witness. We have a binder for the Trial Chamber and for our colleagues in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, could you please look at document under Roman numeral I, item one -- item 1, and the number of this document is 1749. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, is this a document from your brigade?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have just been telling us about the problems you had with replenishment. If you look under item 2, would you say that the item describes those problems that you experienced at the beginning which was due to the make-up of the population?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes. When men joined the army, they abandoned their cattle and their field and they didn't have anything to live on, either them or their families.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was the Croatian population from the area also mobilised into your brigade? If not, how were they mobilised?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: When it came to the 306th Brigade, we did not mobilise Croats because they had managed to establish their own units and commands, so they were already deployed and assigned to their units. We lagged behind them in our own organisation and in setting up our units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, you -- you've told us that you did not have enough professional officers and educated men. You became the brigade commander. And although you were a professional soldier, what duties were you assigned to before you joined the brigade? Were you qualified to become the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: I said that I didn't have enough professionally educated men, especially to fill up command posts. I can illustrate that by my own example. I was very young. I was not a very experienced officer. I was only 30 at the time. My military experience was anything but rich. Before I joined the BiH army, I was the deputy commander of a command post of a company in the Republic of Slovenia. And we all know what a brigade is, and we all know how experienced an officer has to be in order to become a brigade commander. First of all, he has to have a rank, either a lieutenant colonel or a colonel, and I didn't have that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, if you look at the following document, number 2, and especially its part talking about materiel and technical equipment. And the number that the document bears is 1753. In addition to the problems that you had with the mobilisation of people, did you have any other problems and does this document reflect your problems on the 28th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the situation on the 28th of March, 1993. This report, I would say, is a somewhat optimistic reflection of the situation, which must have been even worse. But let's say that we can accept this as a realistic reflection of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, did the situation in the 306th Brigade improve throughout the year, or did you encounter even bigger problems when it came to the replenishment of the brigade and its equipment?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: I hoped that with time the situation would improve; however, as time went by, the situation got worse by the day, by the minute, especially for my brigade, because we did not have any means to obtain equipment, to service what we had, and that was broken and the situation got worse.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where was the command of your brigade? Where were the command posts of your battalions? First of all, how many battalions did you have and where were their commands?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: The 306th Brigade had four battalions on its strength. The brigade command was in the Bila mine, in Han Bila, and in the administrative building of the mine. The 1st Mountain Battalion of the 306th Brigade was deployed, and its command post was in Mehuric in the primary school there. The 2nd Mountain Battalion of the 306th Brigade was in Krpeljici in a house there which serviced as the community reading room. The 3rd Battalion was in Han Bila, in the primary school there. And the 4th Battalion was deployed in the village of Visnjevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where were the troops billeted? Were they billeted in barracks, as would be customary for a military unit?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: The troops that were not on the defence lines facing the Serbs were staying at home, in their own houses. All but some men from the 1st Battalion; those people were billeted in the school. This is where they stayed. This is where they lived. This is where they rested.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the location of the defence line where you were? How big was that line? How long was that line, especially in terms of the size of your unit and its level of equipment?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: The 306th Brigade was on Mount Vlasic on the defence line facing the Serbs. The height of that mountain is around 1600 metres. In the winter it was cold. In the summer it was hot. Our defence line was up to 25 kilometres long. All of us soldiers know what would be the optimum length of the defence line for a brigade to be able to put up an efficient defence. It should be five to six kilometres. We had a very long line and we adjusted our means to that line.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have just told us, Mr. Sipic, that the situation got worse by the day. Can you please look at the document number 4, and the number is 0930881.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the second paragraph after item 2, "Armed forces." The first words are "logistical support."

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read this and can you tell me whether what it says here in this report reflects the deterioration of the situation in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: "The logistical support of the unit is bad. We have been prevented from performing our regular duties because we don't have enough fuel, lubricants, and spare parts for the vehicles. We don't have enough ammunition or clothing. We have already drawn your attention to that. The link with the command post of the OG has not existed for the last ten days. This should be resolved urgently," and so on and so forth. Do you want me to go on reading?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I would just like to ask you whether this reflects the situation that you have already described and the deterioration of the situation in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does. I have already testified about that. I have said that as time went by, the situation got worse by the day, and this is reflected in the report that I have just read out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the document after number 5. The number is 1821. And if you look at this part in B/C/S, the fifth line from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this part, we can see your request that some of your troops should be relieved and replaced by some other troops in -- from the region. Is this your warning that the unit was not in the position to perform its duties because of the problems that it was facing, or was the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. situation in the brigade at the beginning of May maybe better?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: The situation was as is described in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the problems that you have briefly described for us, tell me, Mr. Sipic, did you as a commander take any steps firstly to train your soldiers; secondly, to discipline your soldiers? What were the -- what were the conditions like and what -- how did you try to do that?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: I was aware of the situation in the brigade, and we did not sit and wait for the situation to be resolved on our behalf. We tried and do whatever we could within our limitations. As far as the brigade command is concerned, we organised some training for all the bodies of the command. We involved the subordinate battalion commands. We asked them to carry out certain training of the non-commissioned officers who could then work as platoon commanders. We did that in order to soldierise the strength of the 306th Brigade as best as we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the document that we have just seen, you described the inability to communicate with the West OG. Tell me, please: What were the links and communication like in the first half of 1993 with your superior commands and with your subordinate units? When was it approximately when you began having somewhat more stable links?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Throughout the entire period from January to mid-July, our communication with the superior command was almost non-existent. Sometimes it was impossible to communicate with the West OG, so we used the command of the 3rd Corps in order to obtain information and to forward some information from the 306th Brigade. It was only when the Bosanska Krajina OG was established and we joined this OG, our links became somewhat more efficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at document after number 4, bearing number DH0831.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after number 4. We're going a bit back. You're saying here in the last sentence: "The reason is that we are 13 kilometres away from Travnik and we don't have the means to send our courier three times a day." Does that mean that you did not have means even to establish a courier link? What communications means did you have at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Well, yeah, this is correct. We did not have any means of communication, wire or wireless. At that time, we did not have any vehicles or fuel in order to be able to establish a courier link as a last resort. We had very poor communications links. The strongest communication link was RUP 12. Those people who are familiar with the army will know what RUP 12 is. This was a customary link between the commander of the company and the commander of a platoon. Its range, the range of this radio set, is very short and that's why it was normally used by tactical groups at lower level.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive the package communication link at any point in time? And for how long did you have it? Why didn't you use it for any longer?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: After I -- complaints and -- we received the package communication, which broke down, we had this type of communication only for 10 or 15 days. We tried to take the equipment for servicing to Travnik. The person who could deal with that problem could not come to our command post. He asked us to bring the radio set to Travnik. As we were transporting the radio set to Travnik, we were stopped at the HVO checkpoint and it was -- this radio set was seized from us, and from then on we never had a radio package.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at document number 8. The number is 1854. The date is 30 May 1993. Do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the document and tell me whether this document describes this problem of yours involving the package communication set that was seized from you.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is exactly what the document describes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, on several occasions you have mentioned the OG West. Tell me, which was your superior command, the superior command of the 306th Brigade, and for how long?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: When the 306th Brigade was established in November 1992 up to March 1993, the first superior command was the command of the 3rd Corps. After the subsequent reorganisation and changes in the command structure of the BiH army and OGs were established on the strength of the 3rd Corps. In the territory of Bugojno, the West OG was established, and from then on this was the first superior command to the 306th Brigade. This was from March 1993 up to June 1993. After that, after June 1993, the first superior command to the 306th Mountain Brigade was the Bosanska Krajina OG.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A little while ago you said that you made efforts to train your men and that this was rather difficult in spite of all your efforts. Please look at the document in tab 9, 1874. This is an order of the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, yes, this is an order of the 306th Brigade in which you order the way in which reports are to be made pursuant to the order of the Bosnian Krajina OG. Tell me, these efforts to train the operations and training organ as to how the superior command was to be reported to in June, does it illustrate the problems you have testified about and were the efforts made to train your staff made only in a limited period of time or did they extend over the entire period?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, from June -- or rather, from the time when the brigade was established until June, the method of reporting had not yet been agreed on, that is, reporting by the unit to the superior command, and this confirms what I have already said about the kind of officers and the kind of staff appointed to the brigade. This is yet another effort to explain to people how they should report to the superior command. We made such efforts daily. For as long as I was the brigade commander, I saw that people didn't really know how to do things, so we had to train them, advise them, inform them to the best of our ability as we went along.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, you are speaking of continual problems. You were the commander. The commander had significant authority. Tell me, why didn't you simply ask for trained men? Were you able to do that? Were there such men available? Or did you have to do this as you went along, training people on the job?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we were forced to use these people because the Secretariat for National Defence of Travnik Municipality did not have a sufficient number of men available who had military training. We did ask our superiors whether there were any men available who were qualified and trained in order to fill the officer's posts, but this was a very serious problem in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina since we did not have sufficient officers who were already trained.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, we will now move on to another topic. You said that the Croat population organised themselves before you did into units of the HVO. Tell me, first of all, what were the relations between your brigade and the HVO, whether any problems arose in those relations and when.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: From the very beginning, when the brigade was established, there were certain problems with HVO units, primarily relating to their checkpoints which were set up all along the valley. Wherever there was a Croatian village, there was a checkpoint. That's where most of the problems arose. There was mistreatment, and I can't even remember the number of occasions on which I was checked, questioned by lower-ranking officers and soldiers, mistreated, and so on. The situation grew worse in January, in the latter half of January, when an announcement was made on the media that all members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina should place themselves under the command and control of the so-called Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and those who did not do so would be disarmed. Believe me, this was such a shock for all the members of the army and for the entire Muslim, Bosniak population because we had never dreamed that such a thing might happen. We truly considered them to be our allies. We thought we could count on them participating in a joint struggle against the Serbian forces. Believe me, this was a terrible time for everyone in that valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, would you please look at tab 2, the document -- or rather, the document behind tab 1 in section 2, and this is document DH0588. In the paragraph before the last --

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It says "January," and then number "one," have you found this?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: January.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then under number 1 is DH0588.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at the paragraph before the last, and in it the second sentence. "Besides this, the commander of the Travnik HVO informed us of the order of the HVO of the so-called Herceg-Bosna about putting all the units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina under the command and control of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." Was this ultimatum made known to you officially at a meeting?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. We had a meeting in order to resolve certain problems in Travnik municipality. And at this meeting, we were officially told by HVO officials that we should act in compliance with this order by the top leadership of Herceg-Bosna. We were amazed when we heard this and when we received this information officially. Our standpoint, however, was clear and unambiguous, and that was that we would carry out only the orders of our superior command, the command of the 3rd Corps, regardless of the HVO ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with possible conflicts, were there any open-armed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. conflicts in your area? And did they influence the situation in the area where your brigade was?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes. Open clashes between the HVO and the army had already taken place in Gornji Vakuf and Novi Travnik. Believe me, this had a major impact on my brigade and my men, and we were very concerned. We wondered where all this was leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of this situation, Mr. Sipic, did you know what the orders of your superior command were in connection with these conflicts and were any orders issued to you in relation to this and to what extent did you comply with these orders?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. We had explicit orders from the commander of the 3rd Corps that we constantly had to comply with all agreements and that we must never enter into an open clash with HVO units; that we should do everything possible to avoid such clashes; and if we were attacked directly, only in that case could we respond and enter into a conflict. Otherwise, we were by no means to enter into a conflict with them and we complied with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of these orders coming from the 3rd Corps, did you take any steps in your brigade, and was the aim of these to prepare for defence or was it to prepare for a possible conflict?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. We constantly had precautions. We were organising defence from the Serb forces, and we always had to have sufficient forces to prevent a breakthrough of the Serb forces from the Lasva area. Also, part of the men were on the alert in the villages should there be an open conflict with the HVO and an HVO attack on our villages or the members of the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, would you please look at the documents in tab 2. One is 1723 and the other one, 725.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are these orders issued by you in which, for the sake of precaution, you envisage a certain combat situation in the brigade while saying that the brigade was not to cause a conflict?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was one of the measures. Putting the commander at the ready. This is an order issued by me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, you mentioned Gornji Vakuf and Novi Travnik. Tell me, were these places where there was an open conflict near the territory of your brigade? And did this cause concern that the conflict might spread to your territory?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: You know that the Bila Valley is 15 to 20 kilometres away from Novi Travnik, and it was to be expected that the conflict would spread to the Bila Valley area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, the situation that prevailed in January, did it calm down, and in later months, in April, did the threat of a conflict with the HVO vanish or did something else happen?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: On the contrary. Instead of calming the situation down, there were new flashpoints, new offensive activities by the HVO which opened up a conflict in the Vitez area, where units of the 325th were attacked and the inhabitants of predominantly Bosniak villages. There was an unfortunate event in the village of Ahmici, which additionally worsened the situation and brought it to boiling point.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, did you regularly report to your superior command about all these events?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes. We constantly sent daily reports on all the problems and all the events that took place to our superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you now, please, look in the section entitled "April," in tab 1, documents 2, 3, and 4 -- or rather, in -- the numbers are 1758, 1762, 1764, and DH0832. And tell me, please: Does this illustrate the way in which you reported to your superior command on events in relation to the HVO and do they mention the events that took place in that period on your brigade's territory in the Bila Valley?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And these orders confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After these reports in number 4, would you look at this document, number 4, DH0832.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as we can see, this is a report from the intelligence organ. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. This is a collective intelligence report pertaining to the previous period and events in the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of page 2 of this document, you evaluate the ability of the HVO in the Bila River Valley and about their good logistical support, but there is a sentence that mentions the road communications. What happened? Why did you mention this fact in your report that they are constructing a road in this area? Who was constructing a road? Through what villages? And what effect did this have on your men?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. I wrote this for the following reason: As the HVO had organised checkpoints on all public roads leaving the Bila River Valley in the direction of Travnik, to hinder movement for members of the army and the population of the valley, they constructed an alternative road which members of the army could neither control nor obstruct, and they linked up all the villages where there was a Croatian population in order to make it possible for their forces and men to move without any hindrance. They simply bypassed the existing road communications in order to be able to perform all their tasks without any hindrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On page 2, in the next paragraph, you mention elevation 1486, where they could fire on the valley. Tell me, on which positions were HVO forces deployed in the valley? And what does this statement of yours mean in your report to the superior command?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: As I've just said, the defence line of the 306th Brigade toward the Serb forces was 25 kilometres long. Here we were trying to say that the HVO, which had one HVO brigade in Travnik municipality and another one in the Bila River Valley, and they held only 500 to 1.000 metres facing the Serb forces, and they had all their other men at their disposal, and they used them to deploy them behind our lines. They took up dominant facilities, including this one, where they put artillery weapons on the elevation in order to control the valley. Then they built fortifications and engineering work near all the villages where there was a majority Bosniak population. They started preparing on time, especially in the Bila Valley. And this is what we reported on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Prosecution has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just note for the record that page 2 of DH832 does not seem to be translated into English, at least not in the binder that I have. So that all the information pertaining to the road which the witness was just asked about and -- and the paragraph after that, we don't seem to have an English translation of page 2 of this document, at least in the materials that we were provided with today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have noticed that when you mentioned that elevation point there's no English translation of the last bit of that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my legal assistant has just drawn my attention to that same thing. This must be due to either printing or something. There is a translation, I'm sure. We shall try and see by the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But you do not have the entire document, and this is what our learned friend has drawn our attention to. I apologise. I have not compared the originals with their translations before I distributed my binder. But before the end of the day today or tomorrow morning at the latest we will, I'm sure, be able to provide you with the rest of the English translation. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, you said that in mid-April there were combat activities in the region of Vitez and in the Lasva Valley, and you have emphasised the village of Ahmici. Can you tell me, where were your troops deployed at the time and how did you deploy your troops?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, one part of the 306th Mountain Brigade was deployed on the defence line facing the Serbian forces and the remainder of the troops I had to regroup, and I had to move all of them towards Vitez because there was a realistic danger that some of the conflict from Vitez will spread on to the Bila Valley. As the brigade commander, I had to bring some of my troops into the state of readiness in that area in order to prevent possible enemy moves. The situation was even more compounded by the fact that there were refugees in the Bila Valley, and they kept oncoming and passing through the Bila Valley because this was the only place where they found a safe haven for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, can you tell us briefly what happened in May in the area covered by your brigade. Did the situation improve? Did it become stable? Or did it become even worse?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: In the month of May, there were even more incidents. Every day there was an incident, there was a skirmish, there were killings of the command members at the command post. Sniper fire was opened every day on the neighbouring villages. In the month of May, the entire Bila Valley was encircled. Part of it was encircled from the Mount Vlasic by the Serb force and then from the Zenica, Novi Travnik, and Nova Bila, that's where the HVO forces were. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And we were completely encircled in the Bila Valley at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at tab entitled "May 1993." There are a number of documents there from 2 to 22. I'm going to ask you to look at these documents, and can you tell us what these documents are about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe the witness can do that during the break. It is quarter to 4.00. Colonel, we will have to take a technical break. During the break, maybe you can have a look at the documents that the Defence has just mentioned. We shall resume at ten past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I hope, Mr. Sipic, that you have managed to look at the documents I asked you to look at, from 2 to 22.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: I did not take the documents with me. They -- they've stayed here all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the documents now. I was hoping you might be able to look at them during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps while the witness is looking through the documents, it might be helpful if the numbers were read into the record by my learned colleague, because of course several weeks or months from now when we review the transcripts, we don't know what documents 2 through 22 will be, and so perhaps she could -- if she could do that while -- while he's looking at them, that might be helpful for the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could you please read out the numbers of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I've asked the witness to look at the following documents: 1824, DH0976, 1827, DH0986, number 1830, number 1831, number 1832, number 1835, DH1001, DH1011, number 1839, DH1014, DH1013, number 1021, DH1020, number 1842, number 1844, number 1848, number 1851, number 1064, and number 1858.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Some of the documents have already been admitted, and documents like, for example, 184 are the ones that have been marked for identification. In the list, there is a document that hasn't been translated into English; that is 1064, which is only in B/C/S, as we can see from your list. According to the Defence, these documents will illustrate the developments that took place in May 1993. I believe that the witness has had the time to look at the documents. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, first of all, tell me whether you recognise these documents as documents that you personally drafted, either you or members of the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In these documents, did you describe incidents that took place in the area covered by your brigade and involving the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes. Every day we described what was going on in the Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, we have seen some documents that were typewritten, but there are some others which are either telegrams or handwritten documents. Tell me why there is no uniformity in these documents, why there was no customary way of reporting to your superior brigade.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: This arose from the very specific situation that we were in. I've already testified about our communications means, which were practically non-existent, so there was no way for us to communicate. That is why we sent coded telegrams to our superior command. When the superior command was not in its command post, when the command post was moved, that person did not have anything but a piece of paper and a pencil, and that's how they drafted reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: These numerous problems, incidents, blockades, the fact that the brigade was encircled - and all this is described in the documents that you have just looked at - did all this have an impact on the morale of your men and their combat readiness?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: All of the developments and events that are mentioned in these documents had a big impact on the morale of the members of the 306th, because all of these developments were taking place very close to either them or their families and that's why they exerted a huge impact on their morale and combat readiness. As far as combat readiness is concerned, one can see from the documents that the combat readiness of our men was at a very low level. From the month of May, the unit could not be sent to a mission as a whole. The movement was restricted. People could not move from one village to another. And that is why the unit was active in those areas where its members happened to be. That's how the unit functioned. And part of the command was transferred and its work covered the whole territory of the Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, did your men point to the problems that their families might have had? Did you come across the problem of men refusing to go to the line, or did they maybe go to the line without any objections?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you that the members of the 306th Brigade were very poor. They didn't have any food. They were poor and they still had to be sent to the lines on the Vlasic plateau. They did not leave their wives and children behind easily, because their families were at a constant risk of attacks and other things. Sometimes we even had to punish our soldiers for failing to report when they were called to the lines. This was a very complex and specific situation during that period of time, both in the 306th Brigade and in the entire Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, where were you at the beginning of June?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Not only at the beginning of June, but from the last part of May onwards I was in the village of Krpeljici. On that particular day, we had a meeting in Guca Gora with the representatives of the HVO and civilian bodies of power from Travnik municipality. The goal was to overcome the existent problems and difficulties. On that day, during the break I went to have a coffee in Krpeljici, which is the village next to Guca Gora. And while I was there, the entire Bila Valley was blocked and nobody could move. Nobody could pass through the Bila Valley. A member of the HVO informed me that I was not to leave the place where I was because anybody at any of the HVO checkpoints could arrest me. That's why I stayed in Krpeljici village for a somewhat longer period of time, until the moment I handed over my duty as the brigade commander. All this time I was in Krpeljici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What about the rest of the command? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: I'll try and reconstruct the situation. It was a long time ago. I may not be able to remember all of them. However, the -- I'm going to mention the key figures. I, as the commander, and Chief of Staff, Remzija Siljak, and the assistant for finances, Mujo Husanovic, as well as with my assistant for morale, Halem Husic, we were in Krpeljici. The other part of the command, with Mustafa Fazlic, who was the assistant commander for training, was in Mehurici. The assistant commander for logistics, Munir Karic, he was also in Mehurici at the command post of the 1st Battalion. I was in Krpeljici at the command post of the 2nd Battalion. Some other officers who were in charge of mobilisation and organisation, Halihodza [phoen] Omer, was in Alihodzici, the logistics officer was in Mosor, and one part of the officers had remained in the main command post in the mine. This is where the assistant commander for security, Asim Delalic, was, as well as the officer for operations, Husic. Those are the ones that I remember. I believe that if I saw documents, I would be able to remember some others. But these were the key figures and this is where they were at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Having looked at the 22 documents, I'm sure you can see that the situation was very dramatic. Tell me, did you receive any order from the 3rd Corps or did you yourself decide to prepare for a defence in case there was an open conflict in the territory covered by your brigade?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Our commander, our corps commander was a very responsible person. He received information every day. And he had -- he ordered us to come up with three scenarios. One of them envisaged an attack by the Serb forces. The second one envisaged an attack by the HVO. And the third one envisaged an attack from both sides. At that time, this was a realistic situation where all the three scenarios could have taken place. And we did it. We drafted our plans and we submitted them to our superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: In June was there occasion for you to act pursuant to this order, or did the conditions you found yourself in dictate something else?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: We drew up these three scenarios, but they were never implemented. According to these reports, the situation changed from day to day, and from day to day new decisions had to be made, new procedures put in place. I had no communication with the commander. My command had no communication with the superior command. Communication was very difficult. We simply had to adapt to the situation as it arose in the Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now briefly explain what the situation dictated to you in early June as the commander. What happened to your men, to the encircled villages, and what were the moves made by the HVO at that time in relation to your forces? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: As I was where I was, not at my command post, and it was very difficult for me to communicate with the rest of my command, although my chief means of communication was only a RUP 12 - and I have explained what the characteristics and possibilities of a RUP 12 are - I received a telegram saying that the village of Ricica in the immediate vicinity of Han Bila was encircled and that an ultimatum had been issued to the population to hand over their weapons and abandon their village. The village of Radojcici had been attacked. This was very close to the village of Ricica. On the 3rd of June, I received an alarming request saying that the village of Velika Bukovica had been encircled and had been issued with an ultimatum to surrender and disarm by nightfall on the same day. The villages of Ricica, Radojcici, and Bukovica were asking for assistance. As these villages were part of the 2nd Battalion's territory, I was with the commander of the 2nd Battalion. Ricica and the Radojcici were on the territory of the 3rd Battalion. So I told the commander of the 2nd Battalion to sent a small unit in the direction of Bukovica. However, this was not possible because his battalion numbered very few men in the village of Krpeljici because other parts of his battalion were in other villages. So he was unable to respond. I asked a part of the command, the part that was in Mehurici, to see whether it was possible to find a way to send assistance to the village of Velika Bukovica and to inform the command of the 3rd Corps of the situation and also to ask any humanitarian organisation or UNPROFOR to urgently come to the village of Bukovica because we could expect something terrible to happen there at any moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Was there any movement of these forces from Mehurici where part of the command was in the direction of Velika Bukovica and was there any assistance from UNPROFOR at the time when you requested it?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: There was no assistance either from UNPROFOR or any other international organisation. One morning - that's between the 7th and the 8th - I was still asleep. This was in the village of Krpeljici. In the early morning hours, I was awakened by heavy gunfire. I didn't know who was shooting at whom. I thought first that we had been attacked by the Serbian forces or perhaps the HVO. The village was being shelled from all sides. In my immediate vicinity, a house burst into flames. A barn caught fire. I had no information as to what was happening. I composed a telegram and sent it to the command at Rudnik and at Mehurici telling the commands to tell the superior command that we were being attacked from all sides, that we didn't know who was attacking us, and that we were asking for help. The situation appeared to be very dramatic, and I saw no way out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of that day - you say this was the morning of the 8th of June - did you learn what was happening and who told you this?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: There was fighting on all sides. The entire valley was in flames. There was shooting everywhere. You couldn't tell who was shooting at whom. I went to a shelter because there was shelling and my command post could be shelled. Sometime in the early afternoon a member of the 17th Krajina arrived. He was a member of the reconnaissance platoon, his nickname was Zenga. And he arrived at my command post. And of course I asked him what was going on, and he told me that our forces were fighting in order to help the forces in the direction of Mehurici and Velika Bukovica. In the late afternoon, he passed -- or rather, my assistant for logistics, Munir Karic, came along, and he said that they had decided to help the forces in Velika Bukovica. He said he didn't have much time to talk to me. He said there were many casualties, dead and wounded, that he urgently had to go to Mehurici to carry out evacuation, to provide assistance, and to take people in the direction of Zenica. That's what I learned on that first day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: According to this first information you received, what was the direction taken there by parts of the 306th Brigade from Mehurici? Were they going in the direction of Bukovica or in some other direction? And where did they stop on that day?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: They were moving towards Bukovica under the foothills of Mount Vlasic in the direction of Gornje Maline, Bukovica, Radojcici, those villages. And on that day that's where the lines stopped, Bukovica, Radojcici, Maline. That was the line on the 8th that was reached on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you had already learned that our forces were successful and that they were pushing back the HVO units, tell me, did you then take any steps in order to link up the forces? And if so, who went out onto the ground to find out where individual units were?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: As I received reports on that day from Velika Bukovica that we had 18 dead in the village of Bukovica and 5 wounded, that the village had been torched, that members of the HVO were using a human shield of the civilian population, and that they had taken them to Nova -- Stara Bila. During the day, there had been an attack in the direction of the villages of Bandol and Mosor, and I received urgent requests from my forces for assistance. As the situation was what it was, I had only one officer available whom I could send in that direction to coordinate and join up the forces, and this was Remzija Siljak, my Chief of Staff. He went out onto the ground in order to see what the situation was, to link up the units, and to -- to lead the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, on the following day, did any members of the units from Travnik arrive at your command post, and had they started out in response to your appeals for help?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: As I had asked for help everywhere, from anyone who could offer help, to -- when the village of -- when the village of Bukovica was liberated from the siege, they were able to go in the direction of my units. And on the following day, the Chief of Staff of the 312th arrived at my command post, and he told me that part of his forces from the 312th and part of the forces from the 17th Krajina and from the 7th Muslim from the direction of Travnik had arrived in the area of Velika Bukovica and that it was necessary to link up these forces. I looked at the map with him to see where these units were and how far they had arrived -- come, and we tried to agree joint activities by these units. And at around 3.00 or 4.00 I received news that this Chief of Staff had been killed out on the field in his effort to link up these forces. He was killed out there. And this all shows how difficult it was, how impossible it was in that situation to establish joint operations and control and to link up the forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, on the following days, your forces, which had come as far as Guca Gora, did they fight in Guca Gora? Did they come up against any resistance? And where were your forces moving on the following days, the 9th and the 10th?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: As we had received certain intelligence reports from the assistant for intelligence, we learned that Guca Gora had been abandoned and that there were no HVO members or men there. I ordered the commander of the 2nd Battalion to enter the village of Guca Gora with a view to protecting the Franciscan monastery in Guca Gora, to secure it. And as we had information that this had been the command post of the Frankopan Brigade, to secure this command post and to establish outside the village of Guca Gora -- or rather, that they were to go as far as they were able to until they came up against HVO resistance, and in this way to see where the HVO had established their lines. In the meantime, in Perici, I was still commanding the commanders of the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, did you join up with part of your command at some point? And if so, when was this?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: In view of the situation and the impossibility of communicating or moving by motor vehicle, after all this - and I can't remember precisely whether it was on the 11th or the 12th of June - a part of the brigade command managed to gather together after being separated for some 10 or 15 days and not acting jointly as a command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that your units passed through Guca Gora and went in the direction of the newly established HVO lines. At that point, how well equipped were your units? After this fighting, did they have sufficient means to continue fighting?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you that in our previous fighting, the equipment and materiel we had had had been spent more or less. Let me just tell you that on the average, at least according to the reports from Fahir Camdzic, the battalion commander, he said that on the average his soldiers had 10 to 15 bullets. And those were the circumstances under which they were to continue fighting because we had no way to replenish these supplies and no way to bring any supplies to the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, would you please look at the tab entitled "June 1993," and will you please look at the documents numbered from 1 to 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would again ask if perhaps my colleague could read the numbers into the record and also indicate which documents we're missing translations of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Would the Defence please respond to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The documents are 1094, which is only in B/C/S; document 1105 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please tell us what document is under 1094.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an operative report for the 1st of June, 1993. These are various documents pertaining to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. month of June issued by the 306th Brigade. Document 1105 also exists only in the B/C/S version; it is a daily operative report for the 3rd of June, 1993. Number 3 is document 1864; number 4 is document 1867. This is also only a B/C/S version. It's a telegram reporting on the situation of the 2nd of June at 21.15 hours. The next document is 1869, 1880, 1881, 1882, 1883, 1884, 1886, 1889, 1893, and document 1902.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, do you recognize these documents as documents issued by your brigade? Were these documents sent by you or persons subordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are these documents reporting on a certain situation obtaining on the territory of your brigade from the 1st of June?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes. Probably because of the situation the person compiling these documents didn't have all the necessary information because even worse things happened to us as a brigade on the entire territory of the Bila Valley. However, they sent only the information they were aware of at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said the person at the basic command post compiled information known to that person. If I understood you correctly, this would be at Rudnik?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how did you communicate with this basic command post? What was your method of communication with them?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: It was very poor. Sometimes I managed to send a telegram through the RUP 12, but most of the time I had no communication at all with this basic command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In some of these documents, there is mention of the appeals for help you sent to the superior commands. Did you forward these requests to the basic command post and did then they send them on, or did you send them to the superior command directly?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Part of my appeals for help were sent to the basic command post, and then the officer at the basic command post would forward them on to whomever he was able to communicate with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As the documents were for the most part drawn up at the basic command post, were you able to learn all the information contained in these telegrams that were sent to the superior command at the time these events took place, or were you informed of these events later on?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Not a single telegram sent while I was in Krpeljici during those 15 or 20 days was something that I knew about. I didn't even know what was in the reports sent to the superior command. I was able to learn this only when the command was again reunited at a single command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The documents sent from your brigade, if you compare them with any normally functioning brigade, to what degree do they deviate from the normal methods of communication and the normal possibilities of a commander to establish command and control over his units and inform his superior command of this?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: This situation was absurd. These means of communication and this method of communication is something that was already outdated in World War II, this kind of communication. Every one of these telegrams had to be written, drawn up, and it's a question of who did that, and then they had to be encoded by hand and then decoded. As for the situation, at the basic command post they were under constant fire. The members of the HVO had positions in the immediate vicinity of the command, and they constantly opened fire in an attempt to take the command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sipic. Tell me now: When did your command join up again? You said that you had a meeting of part of the command, the narrow circle. When was the entire command reunited?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: At that first meeting, I ordered all my assistants and the Chief of Staff to inform all the command officers that they were to gather together on the 18th or the 19th of January in the village of Krpeljici, where I had the command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, given all that the brigade went through in the month of May and at the beginning of June, how long did it take you to re-establish the brigade and to restore it to the situation that was before the month of May?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I never managed to re-establish the chain of control and command as it should have been and then I was transferred. So during the three months, I did not have an opportunity to re-establish my brigade because of the constant fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have just told us that there was constant fighting. In addition to the line that you had on Mount Vlasic facing the Serbs, where else did your brigade have to fight?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: At the same time, when we held the line facing the Serbs, we had an equally long line facing the HVO. This was a newly opened front line, which was even more difficult than the front line facing the Serbs. Believe me when I say that every day on that line I had one or two dead soldiers. Every day we had to launch a counterattack against the HVO in an attempt to restore our positions and to regain the territories. This was a -- day in, day out. Fire was open everyday from all types of weapons and pieces. Sniper fire was opened on my men, and they found it very difficult to bear. A month would pass before I could relieve my soldiers from the lines. Shifts lasted for a month. They had to sleep in the trenches. They had to be there all the time because I did not have fresh troops that could relieve them. I had what I had, and I had to organise myself accordingly. There were no other troops. I did ask for reinforcement, but I could never receive any reinforcement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, let's move on to another topic. Earlier on you were testifying about mobilisation of the Bila Valley population into different units. In the spring of 1993, did you face the problem of individuals and armed groups? And if you did, can you tell us something about that problem and how did it become a problem for your brigade.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: As I have already told you, several units were replenished from the territory of the Bila Valley, and this made my life much harder because I could not ask for a reinforcement. Everywhere in the world when you -- your unit suffers losses and when you send a request for reinforcement, that request is usually granted. However, I did not have any possibility to do that because there were other units that had to be replenished and reinforced. Members of those units would come to the area -- my area of responsibility and stay there, and I did not have any authority over them. There were even troops that did not belong to any unit, and still they said that they belonged to a certain brigade. They stayed at their homes, and they didn't go to any of the defence lines. There were such cases rather frequently in the Bila Valley in my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since there were rogue individuals and groups present in the area, did you inform anybody about that? Did the situation improve? Or did you continue feeling that problem throughout your stay with that brigade?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: We informed our superior command about this problem. We even informed particular units and we told them that there were some people who said that they belonged on their strength. Whenever we did that, we received a response from those units that those people did not belong to them, that they were rogue individuals, and that they were not under the control of any of the units that we had contacted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, did you face the fact that in your area there were also some foreigners from African and Asian countries? If you did face that fact, when did this happen and what can you tell us about that? What did you learn about these foreigners once you joined the brigade in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: When I became the commander of the 306th Brigade, I was aware of the presence of people from African and Asian countries, of foreigners. As a commander, I was interested in what they were doing there, and I received information that they had arrived in the area in order to distribute humanitarian aid to the Bosniak population of the area and also that they were engaged in religious education. This was the initial information that I received about these people who could be found in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where could they be found? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: According to my information, they were in Mehurici, in the primary school there. In the primary school at Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How long did they stay in the primary school? Were they there permanently, or did they change the place of their stay?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: They stayed in the Mehurici school up to the moment when the brigade was established. Once the brigade was established, my 1st Mountain Battalion [Realtime transcript read in error "Brigade"] was billeted in the Mehurici primary school, and that's where its command post was. Members of this battalion were not locals of the Bila Valley. Most of them had arrived from Krajina and Kotor Varos. They were refugees from those areas. They had been expelled by the Serbs. They were billeted there because this is the only place where they stayed. They did not have any other home in the area, and this -- this is where they were billeted as members of the brigade.
