They had a problem with alcohol. They swore. And that's why these foreigners had left Mehurici and the school and they organised a camp in Poljanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just an error in the transcript. On page 48, line 8, it says: "The 1st Mountain Brigade," and it should be "The 1st Mountain Battalion."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, did there come a time when you saw these people carrying arms? How did you learn about that? Did you see it personally?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: These people were using the same road I used from the direction of Han Bila towards Travnik. I came across these people in Jeep vehicles, and as I was passing them by in my vehicle, I saw that they were carrying long-barrelled rifles, automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have just told us that according to your information, they had arrived as humanitarian workers and religious trainers. Do you know what their relationship with the local population was, and are you aware of any problems that occurred among the local population with regard to these Arab men?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Based on the information that I had, I can say that at the beginning they were engaged in humanitarian activities. They organised schools and religious centres. They were teaching children. However, as time went by, they became more extreme when it came to religious matters. They demanded from the Bila Valley population to follow their codes of behaviour, and this was something that the Bila Valley locals were not familiar with. Some people were put off by such religious practices because this was not something that was traditional and typical of the area. These foreigners tried to impose their customs. And there were even discords in the mosque. There was even an initiative in Kljaci village for the mosque to be divided in two parts. The locals did not want to perform the religious service the way they did. And all of a sudden these people became a problem for the locals.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, did they start influencing men in your brigade? Did they try to recruit younger men, able-bodied men from your brigade?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did experience certain problems, but they didn't ask from us to give our members to them. They had direct contact with the local population, and they invited young men to come to their camp. Those young men were sometimes of age, and they made promises to them. They told them they would give them money, clothes, weapons. And given the economic and general situation in the area, some individuals were attracted by those offers and they did go to their camps -- actually, to their camp. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As this became a problem for your unit, did you inform your superior command about that problem and did you point to the fact that something was happening in the area that was beyond your control and beyond the control of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I informed my superior command about that problem. Since I did not have any authority over civilians who were not members of my brigade, I could only take measures and steps against members of my brigade. Those other things went beyond my authority and my competence, and that is why I believed it was my duty to inform my superior command, because I thought that they were better suited to deal with the problem that I have just described.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, in addition to recruiting young men and dividing population into those who were for them and those who were against them, did you face another problem towards the end of April involving these Mujahedin? And if that was the case, can you tell us what the problem was about?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was on the 25th of April, in the morning, when I arrived at my command post in the mine, in the Han Bila-Rudnik, the duty operations officer, Captain Dervis Suljic, informed me that there had been an incident in Miletici village during the previous night. The Miletici village had been attacked by foreigners. He went there because he resided in the close vicinity of that village, and he told me that his father had also been arrested by these foreigners and that the battalion command came to the rescue of the civilian population. They tried to persuade these foreigners to let the civilians go. The battalion command sent me a report on the event, and on that same day a mixed commission had been set up involving the BiH army and the HVO. The head of the BiH section was General Merdan. They went to investigate to find out what had taken place in Miletici village. Since I was informed by the command of the 1st Battalion and my duty operations officer that no member of the 306th Brigade was involved in the attack on Miletici or any other member of the BiH army, for that matter, I issued an order to my officers to draw up information and to inform the superior command of the matter. And this is the information that we sent to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, can you please look at the last tab, entitled "Foreigners," and can you look at the first document, number 0923, which is only in B/C/S. Can you please put it on the ELMO. I apologise. I believe that maybe somebody from the registry could help us. My colleague has just told me that you do have this document in English. So maybe your English version of the document could be placed on the ELMO. If that is correct, Mr. Sipic, you will be able to keep your B/C/S version before you. Can you tell me now, before we put this document on the ELMO: Did you have any doubt in your mind on that day as to who had committed the crime in Miletici? Did all the information that reached you speak only of the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I had no other information apart from the information I received, and this information indicated that it was the members of the Mujahedin who had done this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have a document of the HVO before you, Central Bosnia operative zone of the 26th of April, 1993. Would you please now look at this document, paragraphs 1 and 2, and tell me whether the HVO was fully aware of who had committed the crime in Miletici.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: It's obvious here and it can be seen from the HVO reports that it was the members of the Mujahedin who had committed the crime, not anyone belonging to the 306th Brigade or the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact that in the joint commission which was established, there were reports, did you also send a report to the superior command about this, and did they request that you undertake certain steps?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: As you know, we did send a report to the superior command in connection with the events in Miletici, and this report contained the information we had available. The security organ also sent a report, and the superior command wrote to the security organ. Based on the reports in which we had indicated the problems that these foreigners were causing, they told my assistant for security that he should attempt to collect as much information as possible about these foreigners, who and what they were, where they were working, and to send any information he could collect about them to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before I put a question to you in connection with this request, tell me, did you have any material or other possibilities to carry out an investigation in that camp, to interview those men or ask them about previous events, either about the recruitment of young men or about the event in Miletici?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. There was no way I could do that. I had no resources that would enable me to do this or to solve all these problems. As commander, I had no authority over these persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, when you received information from your assistant commander for security, who told you that his security organ from the 3rd Corps was asking him for additional information about these persons, do you know whether he attempted to contact them and whether at any point there was any contact with these Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: My assistant for security, Asim Delalic, told me what his orders were from the superior command, that is, that he was to gather certain operative knowledge about these forces and these men, these foreigners in our area. I personally - personally - asked that he arrange for a certain contact with them, for me to go to the camp in Poljanice and to ask the persons responsible there what they were doing, what their aim was, what the purpose of their activity was, and why they were creating these problems in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did you ultimately succeed in establishing contact with them?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Ultimately my assistant informed me that on the 11th we could go to the Poljanice area, and he and I - he was driving - so we set out in his vehicle in the direction of Poljanice. As I am not very familiar with that area in the immediate vicinity of the village of Mehurici and Suhi Dol, my assistant for security knew the road to Poljanice and we set out along that road. When we got close to their camp, we noticed a barrier improvised out of wood and next to it was a guard. The guard was wearing a uniform and carrying a rifle. We came there by car, as far as the barrier, and he raised his hand to stop us. We got out of the car and we asked to be received there. When he saw us in uniform, he took out a whistle and blew it. We didn't know why he was whistling. We expected to be attacked. But some 20 metres away there was an old house, and two uniformed persons got out of -- went out of the house and started coming towards us. I observed that one of these was a bearded foreigner and the other one looked like a Bosnian by his external appearance. When they came up to us, they asked us what we wanted. I introduced myself. I said I was the commander of the 306th Brigade. I said I had come to visit their camp because I needed to solve certain problems that they were creating, taking these civilians, attacking Miletici, and so on. The man next to this foreigner was interpreting, and he told me that his name was -- that he was the emir of the camp, and he said, "What is your business here?" I said, "I've come to talk about problems." And he said that two days previously they had talked with Sefer Halilovic about establishing themselves as the 8th Muslim Brigade Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. directly under the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he said that I had no business there. He said that in two or three days they would go there to finalise their agreement with him. When they explained this to me, they said, "Now you can leave our camp." I was a little frightened. I saw that their attitude was quite hostile and arrogant, so I told my assistant we were going. We left, and I ordered my assistant personally to write up an informative report on our visit to the camp and to tell the superior command what had happened. He told me that he had informed the superior command about this event.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you now look at the last documents in this series of documents. The document is dated the 13th of May, 1993 and the heading is "The command of the 306th Mountain Brigade." Would you please tell me whether this is the document compiled by your assistant for military security and whether this document describes your attempt to establish some kind of relationship with these representatives of the Mujahedin because of the numerous problems to which your attention had been drawn by the superior command.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my personal attempt to try and see what was going on, what the problems were, and what the aim of these forces was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Sipic, would you now tell me: During these combat operations in June that we talked about, did you receive information to the effect that something had happened during those battles that required an urgent investigation?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 11th or 12th, when part of the command gathered in Krpeljici, I briefly asked my subordinate commanders to brief me according to their sphere of competence what the problems were and what was going on. At this briefing, the various officers told me of various problems, and Asim Delalic, the assistant for security, informed me that on the 8th, when combat operations were carried out, some civilians of Croatian ethnicity who had been escorted towards the village of Mehurici by military police of the 1st Battalion were ambushed by foreigners and that some of them were taken off and there were grounds to suspect they had been killed. He said that he had started an investigation and that he would tell me the details when he found out what had happened. I told him that he was to inform the superior command of this event and on completing his investigation, he was to inform me of the results of his investigation. My assistant for security carried out this investigation with his men and with the assistant from the 1st Battalion. This, due to the complexity of the task, lasted for some 10 or 15 days, the investigation, that is. And then the assistant commander for security of the 306th, Delalic, and the assistant from the 1st Battalion came to see me, and they told me that some of the civilians of Croatian ethnicity had been abducted under threat of weapons and taken off somewhere and probably killed. I also learnt from them that members of the 306th had not participated in this, nor had any members of the army. I ordered him to inform the security organ of the superior command of all this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, in this set of documents, the first set of documents, would you look at the document under tab 10. It's 1903, under tab 10, yes, in the first section.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: What number?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: 1903. This is about the situation in the 306th Mountain Brigade. It's a short report of the 306th for the command of the 3rd Corps. Tell me, is this the information you received from your assistant for security that there are indications of the execution of 20 captured civilians and members of the HVO and that investigation is pending? Is this the information you received and forwarded to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sipic. I only have one further question: In view of all these events, tell me, did there come a time when you were commander of the 306th Brigade when these foreigners, Arabs, or Mujahedin, were under the command of your brigade? Did this happen at any point in time? And, secondly, when they left the brigade in mid-August, were they members of the 3rd Corps [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: As a commanding officer, I can assert that while I was commander of the brigade, they were never under the command of the 306th Brigade nor, as far as I know, were they under the command of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sipic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is now time for our break. We shall resume at about 6.00 and then I will give the floor to General Kubura, after which we will have cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is an error in the interpretation. I do apologise for interrupting. Page 57, line 6, I think it is not a good interpretation. I said "and secondly, up to the -- up to mid-August, were they under the command of the 3rd Corps?" I think the interpretation is not correct. My witness did -- the witness did answer the question, because he heard it in the original B/C/S. That's page 57, line 6 and 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is something missing on page 10 -- or rather, in line 10, page 57 -- no, could you please repeat your question and then everything will be clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, I will put two questions to you. First, these foreigners or Mujahedin, at any point while you were commander of the 306th Brigade, were they members of the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: I assert with full liability that as long as I was the commander of the 306th Brigade, at no point in time were they under the command of the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Up to that time, do you know whether they were under the command of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, they were not under the command of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We shall resume around 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now resume, and I give the floor to the Prosecution -- I forgot the other Defence team. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We do have a few questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Sipic.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I'm sorry, I'm not receiving any interpretation and the microphone is not working.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You've told us today that you were the commander of the 306th Brigade of the 3rd Corps from the end of 1992 up to mid-August 1993. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Your brigade was composed of four battalions.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please answer a few questions with regard to the 1st Battalion of your brigade. The headquarters of the 1st Battalion of your brigade, the 306th Brigade, was in the school in Mehurici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said that unlike other battalions, the troops of this battalion were billeted in that school because they were refugees and they didn't have any other home in the area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: How many troops were members of the battalion and how many were billeted in the school in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Most were from Krajina, refugees from Krajina. There were other members from Kakanj and so on and so forth. Not everybody in -- from that battalion was billeted in the Mehurici school. Some were in Zenica and so on and so forth. Some 100 or so men did not have any other accommodation and they stayed in the school. This battalion had about 250 men altogether, and these men stayed across Central Bosnia. Some were in Zenica, some in Kakanj. And those who had families there, when they were free they went there. Those who did not have families in Central Bosnia were billeted in the school in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: So approximately 100 people were there on a permanent basis, in the school in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, I put it to you that in the school in Mehurici there were never members of the 7th Muslim Brigade of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: I would agree with that. I -- to my knowledge, members of the 7th Battalion -- 7th Muslim Brigade were never there in the school in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I also put it to you that the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade was never stationed in Mehurici as an organised unit. They were never stationed in Bila Aragina [phoen]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, this is correct. I don't have any information to the effect of them being stationed in the area of the Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You have told us today that you visited the camp -- actually, you came as far as the entrance to the camp of the foreign fighters. I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. believe that on record we only have the date 11th, but there's no month.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: It was on the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said at the entrance you met with two foreign fighters, and according to you one of them was a foreigner and the other one spoke Bosnian. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: No, it is not correct. One of them was a guard, and he was a foreigner. And the other two, when the whistle was blown, came from the house in Poljanice, came towards us, and one of the two that I -- that approached the entrance spoke Bosnian; therefore, he was a Bosnian. And the other one was a foreigner. And the guard as well was a foreigner.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The persons that you met at the entrance to the camp did not have any insignia showing that they belonged to the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: No. They wore camouflage uniforms without any insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: While you were the commander of the 306th Brigade, in the school in Mehurici foreign fighters were billeted and you found them there when you -- when you came there.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't find them there personally, but I have information that they were there before the brigade was established. Once the brigade was established, then the 1st Battalion was stationed there. They abandoned the primary school in Mehurici and from then onwards the 1st Battalion of my brigade was billeted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that you saw -- saw them personally there but that they were there when the 1st Battalion was billeted there.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: In that case, I didn't understand you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: To Mrs. Residovic's question, you answered that these foreign fighters were never under the control of the 306th Brigade or under the control of the 3rd Corps of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I put it to you, Mr. Sipic, that these foreign fighters who were billeted in the school in Mehurici and those who stayed in the Poljanice camp were never members of the 7th Muslim Brigade and they were never under the control of the 7th Muslim Brigade of the 3rd Corps of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, those people who stayed there were not under the command of those units that you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to go back to the events that you have testified about today, and those events took place at the beginning of June 1993. You have told us that from mid-May 1993 you were in the command of the 2nd Battalion of your brigade, which was in Krpeljici village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And with you there was your Chief of Staff, the Chief of Staff of the 306th Brigade, Remzija Siljak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony, you've also told us that approximately during that period of time the Bila Valley was completely blocked.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: That means that from the command of your battalion in Krpeljici you could not reach your brigade command in the mine.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Not only that. I could not reach any of the villages. I couldn't go to Ricica, or Radojcici, or Bandol, Velika Bukovica, or Mehurici, Alihodzici. All these villages that were in the vicinity, I could not reach. I could not reach any of the villages outside that circle. There was a circle around the entire valley, and there were some smaller circles around smaller points of the territory, depending on where the HVO positions were. The whole Bila Valley was sort of transected and divided into smaller parts which were all encircled.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at the situation that you have just described, one would say that the units that were in the town of Travnik were not able to leave Travnik and reach the Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I've already said that. It was only after the 8th or the 9th that they were able to reach us from the direction of Travnik. There was no chance in hell for them to reach us unless they undertook an air lift and an air drop. They couldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that you know that the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade was stationed in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, that is correct. They were on the strength of the Bosanska Krajina OG and they were subordinated to the Bosanska Krajina OG.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony on page 39, you've told us that on the 8th of June in the afternoon you met with Munir Karic, who was your deputy, the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: No. He was my assistant for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Of the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Of the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And he told you what had happened during that day.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes. He gave me a brief -- a briefing, a very short briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And you told us that Munir Karic told us that parts of the 306th Brigade were engaged on the line towards Gornje Maline, Bukovica, Radojcici, and that's where they reached their final lines. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour, I would like to show the witness three documents. And since these three documents are interlinked, I would like the witness to be shown all the three documents at the same time; this would save us some time. Can the usher please show the witness the following documents: DK22, P579, and P465.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, can you please look at the telegram which was sent by the 306th Brigade to the command of the 3rd Corps. The dates are the 8th of June and the 9th of June, 1993. This is the first document. The first one is P579 and the second one is DK22. In the first, the telegram reads: "We are currently on the line Maline-Guca Gora-Velika Bukovica. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the second, dated the 9th of June, it says at the bottom: "Yesterday our forces reached the line of villages Maline, Guca Gora, Mosor, and Velika Bukovica." My question to you now is as follows: These telegrams that were sent to the 3rd Corps, do they reflect what you were told by Munir Karic on the 8th of June in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, they -- they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, do you know where Hajdareve Njive elevation is?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This elevation is very close to the blue water, to "Plava Voda." As you enter Travnik from the direction of Vitez, this elevation is immediately before the blue waters. This is a restaurant on the right-hand side, and you can see it from the main road some 500 metres from the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: This is in the vicinity of Travnik, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is not more than one kilometre from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the last document, which is a regular combat report of the Bosanska Krajina OG Command, and it was sent to the command of the 3rd Corps. This document is P465. If you look at the last sentence, it says: "The 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade is active on the Hajdareve Njive elevation towards Bukovica."

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I put it to you, Mr. Sipic - and this has been confirmed by some officers of the 306th Brigade, including your Chief of Staff - that on the 8th of June, 1993 the 7th Muslim Brigade was not engaged in combat in the 21 sector of Maline, Bukovica, nor did it operate from the direction of Mehurici towards these settlements.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, what you're saying is correct. I don't have any other information to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: According to the report of the command of the Bosanska Krajina OG to which the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade was resubordinated, which you have just confirmed to us, the 1st Battalion was engaged on the Hajdareve Njive facility, which is some 500 metres away from Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: To Mrs. Residovic's question, you answered that during the next following -- the few following days, the conditions were put in place for the units from Travnik to arrive in this area. If we say "a few following days," that means a few days after the 8th of June, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: This is when members of the 312th Brigade, the 17th Krajina Brigade, and the 7th Muslim Brigade, the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade that has arrived in that area.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: As far as I was informed by the Chief of Staff, who was leaving -- leading this temporary tactical group which was composed of the 312th, parts of the 7th and the 17th Krajina Brigade, they arrived in the Bukovica sector on the 9th. He reported to me and he informed me about that. This is the information that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On the day when you met up with the members and officers of the 312th, the 17th, and the 7th Brigade, the Chief of Staff of the 312th Brigade got killed.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't meet up with all of them. Their representative came to my command post in Krpeljici. He was the Chief of Staff of the 312th Brigade. I did not see any other officers. They remained in the sector, in their areas around Bukovica. He was the only one. He came to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. see me to agree with me on our contacts. They were on our -- on my right flank. On his return, when he was trying to link up all these units, he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And on the same day when you met up with him.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: So the Chief of Staff of the 312th Brigade was killed on that day. This was confirmed to us by the Chief of Staff of the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: It is possible that this was on that date. All I know, that -- I don't know whether it was on the 9th or on the 10th. I don't know. But when he came to see me, on that day, when he talked to me, after he returned he was killed. It is possible that it was on that same day, but it was -- it is not possible for me to remember all those dates. It was a long time ago, but I'm not excluding that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's go back to what you were testifying about when you were answering Mrs. Residovic's question with regard to the events that took place in the village of Miletici. You learned about all that the day after, because you were in Rudnik, in the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't there. On that day in the evening, I was in Travnik. On the next day, when I arrived at the command post of the brigade, I was briefed on what had happened by my duty officer and by the command of the 1st Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It was Suljic Dervis, the duty officer, who briefed you.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that on the same day, the 24th of April, in the command of the 1st Battalion of the 306th Brigade there was a meeting attended by the duty officer who briefed you, Mr. Dervis, as well as Ribo Sulejman from the 312th Brigade and some members of the Mujahedin and that they were negotiating the release of prisoners from the village of Miletici?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. I didn't know what they were talking about. I knew that there were some negotiations, but I'm not personally aware of what you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that on the 24th of April, 1993 members of the 7th Muslim Brigade were not in Miletici?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: According to the information I received from my duty officer and from the subordinate commands and my organ, I did not have any information about this -- or rather, they were not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would now like to go back to the document shown to you by General Hadzihasanovic's Defence. It's the document before last in this bundle. It's 0923. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: What document?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the number at the top is 0923.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: 0923? Yes, I've found it. I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the document that has a translation. The registrar has the translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, we have received the translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we have a copy of that document in English, number 0923.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On top of that. We shall have it put on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You've already seen this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It's an interim report by the chief of the service of the Central Bosnia operative zone. And it says that you as the commander said that the command was helpless in view of the Mujahedin and had no control over them. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Would you look at a sentence mentioning the Chief of Staff of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It says: "The chief of the 7th Muslim Brigade replied that if he's unable to command them and if there is a conflict, let them send their members, the 307th Mountain Brigade, and let them kill them."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The 306th. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you -- this is in this report, and you have just explained.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes. What I explained is all right, but I don't know who this chief is and what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: That wasn't my question.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is what it says. This is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm simply reading out a sentence from the document shown to you by the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you. I will -- I'll return the document to the registrar. And, Mr. Registrar, can we have a copy of this document immediately. I would like the usher to make a photocopy of this document in English immediately. It is half past 6.00. The Prosecution has half an hour. We will then probably continue tomorrow, I suppose. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good evening, Colonel Sipic.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My name is Daryl Mundis, and along with my colleagues here today, we represent the Prosecution in this case. As the Presiding Judge has indicated, we will have some questions for you. And unfortunately, we'll continue into tomorrow. I would like to stress, sir, at the outset that if at any point in time you don't understand my question, simply ask me to rephrase it. My intention is in no way to confuse you, but I'm hoping that you can help us out in terms of providing us with some information on some of the important issues that are at stake in this trial. Let me start by just asking you a few questions that I have that relate to what you've testified about here earlier today. If I understood what you told us, sir, you were the commander of the 306th Mountain Brigade from November 1992 until mid-August 1993.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, once you left the 306th Mountain Brigade, you were then assigned to the Operation Group Bosanska Krajina? Is that -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what position did you hold within the operations group?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Within the operations group, I was the operations officer -- an operations officer in the operations group for a time, until the end of 1993. And in 1994, I was appointed in January assistant commander of the operative group for security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a little bit -- you told us earlier this afternoon about the Mehurici Detachment, which you said was later called Gluha Bukovica. And I believe you said, sir, on page 13 of the transcript, that this detachment wanted to be part of the 314th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, a little bit about what knowledge or information you had concerning the Mehurici Detachment at the time the 306th Mountain Brigade was established in November 1992.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: I had the following information about this detachment: It recruited men from Gluha Bukovica, Zagradje, part of Mehurici, Fazlici, and some other areas in the Bila Valley, and they simply boycotted the brigade. They didn't want me as their commander. They didn't want to be in my brigade. They wanted to be in the 314th Brigade. And the superior command approved their request, so they became part of the 314th Brigade with the seat -- or headquarters in Gluha Bukovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, this unit, the Mehurici Detachment, prior to the establishment of the 306th Mountain Brigade, was that a unit that was part of the Travnik Municipal TO?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes. All these detachments that became part of the 306th Brigade in the Bila Valley had been part of the Travnik Territorial Defence Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In November 1992, can you tell us approximately how many men were in the Mehurici Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Well, this was up to 300 men, not more. I can't be more precise, but it would be about 300. Maybe up to 350.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, the names of any of the commanders or senior leaders within the Mehurici Detachment as of November 1992?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember two: The commander of the detachment was Fahir Camdzic, and in the detachment there was also my assistant for intelligence, Dervis Suljic. I don't remember the others so well, but I remember these two because they were transferred to my brigade. They didn't want to remain in that unit and be part of the 314th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, why the Mehurici Detachment did not want to be part of the 306th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: I didn't talk to them about it personally. They simply refused. My assistants for morale and for security who had the task of seeing what Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was happening simply didn't want to, either because I was the commander or because of the Chief of Staff or some other reasons I'm not aware of, they simply refused. And then we reported to the command that they were refusing. I had only just arrived in that area, and they didn't go into the reasons why. My duty was to establish the brigade. They refused. I informed the superior command. They were given approval to join another brigade. I didn't comment on it, nor did I evaluate these decisions or their merits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel, did it strike you as being in any way odd to you as a professional soldier that this detachment would have some say in terms of what brigade it would form up with?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: The way the situation was then, well, I have been a professional soldier since I was 15. I've been in uniform since then. But this was self-organised. The situation was imposed. The units were not properly established. Certain villages could even say they refused to do this or that and there was no way to make them accept. Our aim was to organise ourselves as best we could, because we saw what was the danger threatening us. We were happy for them to join any unit so that we could use them. As a soldier, I wasn't all that interested into why they wanted to or didn't want to join this or that brigade. I was simply carrying out the assignments and tasks given me by my command. I didn't have time to think about the reasons why. And if the superior command approved this, then probably they did have a good reason. I don't know what it was. Somebody knew something. But I didn't know why they refused. I thought maybe because I had been in the former JNA, because there was hostility toward officers from the former JNA. So that might have been one of the reasons. But I didn't go into it. I didn't investigate it, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I take it though from your answer that Mr. Camdzic and Dervis Suljic did in fact join the 306th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: No. They were mobilised into the Municipal TO Staff. On my arrival, I looked at the men available for the brigade command. I talked to each officer in the brigade command, and the officers I had planned as battalion commanders, I talked to them, and at my proposal they were appointed to new duties and new posts, and they had to hand over their duty to the new officers, and Camdzic was appointed commander of the 2nd Battalion, and Dervis Suljic was appointed. He couldn't just come along of his own initiative. I didn't have anyone better, so I appointed him my assistant for security and intelligence. And that's how it was. It wasn't all that democratic. People couldn't just go and join wherever they wanted to. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question. You told us that from November 1992 through March of 1993 the 306th Brigade reported directly to the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And then upon the establishment of the Operation Group Zapad, your brigade was part of that OG, from March until June 1993.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And then from June of 1993, the 306th Mountain Brigade was part of the OG Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, the date at which the 306th Mountain Brigade shifted from being part of OG Zapad to being part of OG Bosanska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: That was in mid-June. As soon as Travnik was -- the siege of Travnik was lifted, the operative group already existed and the difficulty of commanding part of the 306th and the 312th, in mid-June the corps commander issued an order that the 312th and the 306th should be put under the command of the Bosanska Krajina OG.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you said earlier today on at least two occasions that to the best of your knowledge the foreign fighters, or Mujahedin, were never under the 3rd Corps command. Is that -- is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: That was the information I had as the brigade commander. I was aware of this. I knew they were not. I didn't know what was happening in the 3rd Corps. I can't confirm they were under the command of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My question, Colonel, is: What information do you base this conclusion on?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: I base it on the information. If I was sending reports to the superior command about these problems occurring in the area of the Bila Valley, then the corps commander had competence and had he been able to solve something, he would probably either have ordered me to solve it or he would have taken steps within his competence. I know what the system of command was, and if there was a unit, you had to know who was in command and who was responsible for who. So these are my conclusions as a soldier. It would not be logical if someone was under my command for me not to be able to take certain measures. If I was able to take certain measures, I would do that on my own; if not, I would seek assistance from the superior command. And if they are not under my command, then according to the system of the chain of command -- control and command, my duty was simply to inform the superior command of what was happening and what the problems were in my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On how many occasions, sir, did you discuss the issue of the Mujahedin with your superior commander, whether it was someone from OG Zapad, OG Bosanska Krajina, or someone from the commander of the 3rd Corps, for example?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly how many times it happened. According to the brigade of the 306th Brigade [as interpreted], the superior command was informed and that's the command of the 3rd Corps. And the Operations Group West would find it difficult to be informed because the only communication we had with the Operational Group West was through the command of the 3rd Corps. That's how it was at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, earlier today you described - and this is on page 49, line 20, running through the top of page 50 - you told us about the Mujahedin in effect recruiting or reaching out and trying to take soldiers from the 306th Mountain Brigade. Do you remember testifying about that?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: They were not only from the 306th. They didn't recruit only from the 306th. They toured the villages. The procedure for recruiting is well known. There is a Secretary for National Defence, and every time there is need they will mobilise civilians for a certain brigade and they assign civilians to those brigades. They, however, did something else. They toured the villages and they advertised themselves. They spoke about religion. They said they would help them with material goods. And I'm sure that they found approval of some individuals in the valley. There's no doubt about that, because that's what the situation was. There was no humanitarian aid. Nothing arrived from anywhere. And people accepted anybody who was able to help them survive. And I'm sure that these people benefitted and made the most of that situation of hardship.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, or do you have a rough idea as to the number of soldiers who left the 306th Mountain Brigade in order to join with the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I would say some 50 people left the brigade. I don't know where they went, whether they joined the Mujahedin or not. Very simply put, we just couldn't find these people on their home addresses. I would send military police to find them. If a soldier did not turn up on the defence line and I was informed about that, I delivered the list of the names of those who were missing. I gave it to the military police and sent them to the place where those people resided. But those people were simply not there. We didn't know what to think. They might have joined other units, but there was no way for us to -- to tell. There were no barracks. When they were on leave, they went home; and from home, they could go wherever they wanted. Their rest was 15 days, and during those 15 days of rest they -- nobody could control them. They wore civilian clothes and they could go wherever they wanted. It would have been a different situation if we had had barracks in -- if we had had barracks, they would have been under control. But the situation was different, and our men would go directly from their houses to the line. They would gather in a -- in their villages. A vehicle would come, collect them. They would be transported to the line. And this is the only time when the command had any control over these soldiers and -- but when they were at home, when they were on leave, there was no way to control them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever direct any military police unit or units or military policemen of the 306th Mountain Brigade to go to the Mujahedin camp in Poljanice looking for soldiers who left the 306th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: No. No, I did not have any authority over them. According to the law, I only had authority over my subordinate troops and officers. They could have joined the HVO. We had such cases. If these were my men, I would have had the authority. What I did: I went to their home addresses because those were the places where they resided. What they did, where they went; they could have joined other brigades. Whether they did or not, I didn't know. I did not have any information as to where they went. According to some assessments and what I heard from my assistant commanders, this was a possibility, but I did not have any authority over the camp, so there was no way for me to go there, even with the military police. This was beyond my authority. As a soldier, I knew exactly what my duties and obligations were and what my authorities were as well, as the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you told us that in this type of situation you would send the military police to go to the soldier's home of record. What type of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. authority did you have to visit the homes of these soldiers and to question family members about where they might be?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: I didn't say anything about questioning anybody. When a person is questioned, it is done in a certain way. My soldier, a member of the 306th Brigade who is supposed to go to the defence line, and he didn't go there, pursuant to my chain of command, my subordinate command informed me about those who failed to report for duty. After that, we had to check whether that particular person was home. And when we went home, we rang the bell and we asked for that certain person, mentioning that person's name. And that was it. And if we were told that this person was not home, this is where our authority stopped, because that person could have gone anywhere. That person could have gone across the forest to Zenica. But his options were numerous and he could have chosen any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, just so that I'm clear, then, if a soldier failed to report for duty, the military policeman would go to the soldier's home or home of record; the military policeman would knock on the door; and if the soldier's, for instance, mother answered and said he wasn't home, that would be the end of it and the military police would simply leave the house?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's precisely what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And at no point in time, sir, did any of your soldiers go to the guard at the front gate of the Poljanice camp and ask if any local soldiers from the 306th Mountain Brigade were inside that camp.

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware of any instances where soldiers who had left the 306th Mountain Brigade or any of its subordinate units joined with the Mujahedin and then came back to the 306th Mountain Brigade or any of its subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. I don't have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, if I recall what you told us earlier in response to a question from my learned colleague for the Defence, you told us that this problem of Mujahedin recruiting, if I can use that term, was reported by you to the 3rd Corps Command. Is that an accurate summary of what you told us earlier?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, why did you report this information to the 3rd Corps Command?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Because there were Mujahedin there. We did not have any control over them. And they caused some problems. We asked for our superior command to see who was it who had the authority to solve this problem. Maybe it was the civilian police, politicians, somebody. I don't know. I simply sought ways to deal with that problem, because I didn't have the authority to deal with that problem and I wanted it to be dealt with. And I thought that if I sent accurate reports, I would become part of that solution that I was after.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But, sir, if you told us that the Mujahedin were not part of the 3rd Corps and the 3rd Corps had no authority for the Mujahedin, why would you report this information to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: Do you know what subordination in the army is? I was subordinated to the corps command, and anything that happened in my unit and in the area where it existed, I had to inform my superior command about that, especially if I thought that it was interesting for them to know about those -- about those things. I had to inform them about problems. They were a higher level. They were my superior command. I just informed them. I reported to them. I don't know what they did. I don't know whether they acted on my information. When there was this incident in Miletici, we were asked to collect information on these people, on who they were, what their goal was, what activities were they taking. This is the information that I sent them. And what happened with that information, I don't know. It was not within my purview to follow up on that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, we're just about to the point where we have to break for the evening, but let me ask you a couple of questions about the presence of these Mujahedin -- foreign Mujahedin in the Mehurici primary school. To the best of your knowledge, sir, when did those foreigners leave the school and establish the camp at Poljanice?

utterances.speaker: ESED SIPIC
utterances.text: I joined the brigade at the beginning of November. I didn't go myself to reconnoiter. I wasn't interested in that. I was more focussed on the establishment of the brigade. Once I appointed Mirzet Lubenovic as the commander of the 1st Battalion, he was given the order to station his battalion command at the school. This was sometime mid-November. I don't know exactly when. My goal was to establish the brigade, to establish the battalion, and to billet the battalion somewhere. I suppose that these foreigners just could not agree with these new men who behaved differently, and they simply left without any pressure on our part. I had different things on my mind at the time, so I didn't exactly pay attention to the date when they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think this is an appropriate time to adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 7.00. We will have to stop here. Colonel, I will ask you to come back tomorrow at 2.15. From now onwards you're not supposed to talk to anybody about the case. You are under solemn declaration and you are not supposed to talk to anybody about the case. Tomorrow we shall resume at 2.15, so I invite all of you to be here in the same courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 26th day of January, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.
